raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy for patients with heart failure (HF) who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy but do not meet criteria for, or have not benefited from, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Unlike pacing or CRT, CCM delivers relatively high-voltage, non-excitatory biphasic impulses to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, aiming to augment contractile performance without initiating a new depolarization [1,2]. Early translational work showed that CCM signals can acutely enhance myocardial contractility and, with chronic exposure, improve left ventricular (LV) function and reverse adverse remodeling in canine HF models [1,3]. Mechanistically, CCM appears to influence calcium handling, phosphorylation signaling, and transcriptional programs: human biopsy studies showed improved expression of genes involved in calcium cycling and reversal of the fetal gene pattern, while preclinical studies demonstrated normalization of calcium-binding proteins and sarcoplasmic reticulum regulatory pathways [4,5].

The clinical evidence base began with feasibility and randomized crossover studies in patients with systolic HF, typically narrow QRS complexes, and persistent New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II–III symptoms [2,6,7]. In the FIX-CHF-4 randomized, double-blind crossover trial, 164 patients received CCM-on and sham periods; CCM improved peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores, supporting a symptomatic and functional signal [6]. The larger FIX-HF-5 trial randomized 428 patients with NYHA III–IV HF, LVEF ≤35%, and narrow QRS to optimal medical therapy with or without CCM [8]. Although the trial did not meet its primary ventilatory anaerobic threshold endpoint, it demonstrated improvements in peak VO₂ and quality of life and met prespecified safety boundaries [8]. Subsequent subgroup analysis suggested the greatest benefit in patients with NYHA class III symptoms and LVEF ≥25%, a population that informed later trial design [9].

Meta-analytic data have generally confirmed that CCM improves patient-centered functional outcomes more consistently than hard endpoints. An early randomized-trial meta-analysis suggested improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life without a mortality signal [10]. Special populations have been explored, including patients with atrial fibrillation, in whom earlier atrial-sensing algorithms limited therapy delivery [11]. Experimental and translational studies in rabbit models further linked CCM to SERCA2a/miR-133 signaling, reduced fibrosis, and improved contractile function [12]. Observational series reported sustained improvements in NYHA class, 6-minute walk distance, LVEF, and biomarkers, although these studies were susceptible to selection and survivorship bias [13,14].

The pivotal confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial focused on patients with LVEF 25%–45%, NYHA III–IV symptoms, QRS <130 ms, and no CRT indication [15]. At 24 weeks, CCM improved peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, NYHA class, and quality of life, and reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization, while meeting the device-safety endpoint [15]. Mechanistic reviews emphasize that CCM may be particularly relevant across the HFrEF–HFmrEF boundary because it targets contractile biology rather than electrical dyssynchrony [16,17]. The 2-lead Optimizer Smart system subsequently showed acceptable safety and preserved efficacy, reducing the lead burden compared with earlier 3-lead systems [18]. Individual patient data meta-analysis of prospective studies reinforced benefits in peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and health-related quality of life [19,20].

Patient selection remains the central clinical issue. Contemporary use is best supported in ambulatory, symptomatic patients with LVEF approximately 25%–45%, sinus rhythm or device algorithms permitting adequate therapy delivery, QRS duration below CRT thresholds, and optimized pharmacologic therapy including contemporary foundational HFrEF treatment [21,22]. CCM should not be viewed as a substitute for CRT in patients with left bundle branch block and wide QRS, nor as therapy for advanced HF requiring urgent transplant or durable mechanical support. Practical considerations include venous access, interaction with existing pacemaker/ICD systems, tricuspid-valve lead burden, infection risk, and the need to confirm adequate daily therapy delivery [23,24].

Several uncertainties remain. Long-term mortality benefit is unproven; registry and model-comparator studies are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive [14,20]. Evidence in HFpEF, atrial fibrillation, congenital heart disease, post-transplant graft dysfunction, and cardiomyopathy genotypes is limited to small studies or case reports [25,26]. Recent reviews and meta-analyses underscore consistent improvements in functional capacity but call for adequately powered trials assessing HF hospitalization, mortality, remodeling, device complications, and cost-effectiveness in the era of quadruple medical therapy [27-29]. Current HF guidelines prioritize pharmacologic therapy, ICDs, CRT, transcatheter valve interventions where indicated, and advanced HF referral; CCM occupies a narrower adjunctive niche for persistently symptomatic patients without CRT indications [30]. In summary, CCM is a biologically plausible and clinically validated symptom-improving therapy for selected patients with chronic HF and moderately reduced systolic function, but its role in altering long-term prognosis remains to be defined.
